power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Most children who experience sexual abuse in low-and middle-income countries never receive formal help, but few studies have followed survivors through the steps from telling someone to receiving services.

In this pooled cross-sectional analysis, we combined 15 nationally representative Violence Against Children and Youth Surveys (VACS) fielded between 2013 and 2024 in sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and Eastern Europe to describe this disclosure-andservices cascade and the factors associated with each step.
The analytic sample comprised 3,608 respondents aged 18-24 years who reported sexual abuse before age 18 (2,852 female, 756 male).
We estimated survey-weighted proportions for four steps: told anyone, knew where to seek formal help, sought help (among those who knew), and received help (among those who sought it).
Design-based logistic regression with country fixed effects estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) for individual, family, and community factors.
Overall, 47.1% (95% confidence interval [CI] 44.4-49.7) of survivors had told anyone and 34.8% (32.2-37.5) knew where to seek formal help.
Of those who knew (n = 1,208), 24.8% (20.9-29.1) sought help, and of those who sought help (n = 339), 81.9% (75.9-86.7) received it.
In total, 7.0% (5.7-8.5) of survivors received formal help; this proportion ranged from 0.9% to 26.3% across countries.

Compared with male survivors, female survivors were more likely to tell anyone (aOR 2.30, 95% CI 1.73-3.05) and less likely to know where to seek help (aOR 0.68, 0.50-0.93); among survivors who knew where to go, female survivors were more likely to seek help (aOR 2.66, 1.39-5.09).
Knowing where to seek help was more likely with older age, more schooling, and a living mother.
Survivors who had ever married or cohabited were less likely to have told anyone (aOR 0.75, 0.58-0.96).
No factor other than sex was associated with seeking help among those who knew where to go.
Most survivors are lost before they reach a service: two in three do not know where to go, 45 and three in four of those who know ultimately do not seek help.
Once survivors seek help, most 46 receive it.

Interventions should make services known to young people, particularly those with less 47 schooling, and address the barriers that keep survivors, especially young men, from using services 48 they know about.
Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is a pervasive violation of children's rights and a global public health priority.

In a 2016 analysis of population-based surveys from 96 countries, Hillis et al. [1] estimated that at least one billion children aged 2 to 17 years had experienced some form of violence in the past year.

text.text: Sexual violence is a substantial part of this burden.

text.text: CSA violates the protections guaranteed under the Convention on the Rights of the Child [20] and is associated with long-term harms to physical and mental health [21].

text.text: Prevalence alone does not show whether survivors receive help.
What determines whether a survivor is protected, supported, and able to seek justice is not only whether abuse occurs but whether it is disclosed and followed by an effective response.
Disclosure is often an iterative process rather than a single event [22], and many children who experience sexual abuse do not disclose it [23].
text.formatted: Disclosure is often an iterative process rather than a single event <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref>, and many children who experience sexual abuse do not disclose it <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Systematic reviews consistently identify barriers to disclosure, including shame, self-blame, fear of not being believed, fear of consequences for oneself or one's family, and the relationship to the perpetrator, operating at the individual, family, and community levels [22] [23] [24].
text.formatted: Systematic reviews consistently identify barriers to disclosure, including shame, self-blame, fear of not being believed, fear of consequences for oneself or one's family, and the relationship to the perpetrator, operating at the individual, family, and community levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[24]</ref>.

text.text: In one convenience sample of 42 children and adolescents, recruited mainly through psychiatric, child-welfare, and counseling services, the reported delay averaged about 17 months and ranged from the same day to 10 years [25].
text.formatted: In one convenience sample of 42 children and adolescents, recruited mainly through psychiatric, child-welfare, and counseling services, the reported delay averaged about 17 months and ranged from the same day to 10 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[25]</ref>.

text.text: Retrospective studies of adults indicate that most children who experience abuse do not disclose the abuse during childhood [26].
text.formatted: Retrospective studies of adults indicate that most children who experience abuse do not disclose the abuse during childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Disclosure is the gateway to protection, therapeutic support, and legal redress [23, 24].
text.formatted: Disclosure is the gateway to protection, therapeutic support, and legal redress <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24]</ref>.

text.text: However, when disclosure is delayed or absent, survivors cannot use these routes; current reviews call for earlier disclosure so that support can start sooner [22, 27].
text.formatted: However, when disclosure is delayed or absent, survivors cannot use these routes; current reviews call for earlier disclosure so that support can start sooner <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">27]</ref>.

text.text: To move from documenting how often abuse occurs to identifying where the response system fails survivors, we draw on the logic of the care cascade.
Developed in HIV care as the spectrum of engagement in care [28], the cascade treats help-seeking as a sequence of conditional steps.
text.formatted: Developed in HIV care as the spectrum of engagement in care <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[28]</ref>, the cascade treats help-seeking as a sequence of conditional steps.

text.text: Loss at any step limits the benefit of the steps that follow, so the step with the largest loss shows where intervention is most needed.
Applied to CSA, the cascade comprises four steps: disclosure (telling anyone), knowing where to seek formal help, seeking help from a formal service, and receiving help from a formal service.
The VACS instrument captures each step, which makes it possible to measure how many survivors are lost along the cascade.

In the 2019 Kenya survey, about one third of 18-to 24-year-olds who had experienced sexual violence in childhood knew of a place to seek help (34.8% of females and 34.2% of males), but far fewer sought help (12.5% of females and 3.2% of males) or received help (10.7% of females and 3.2% of males) [10].
text.formatted: In the 2019 Kenya survey, about one third of 18-to 24-year-olds who had experienced sexual violence in childhood knew of a place to seek help (34.8% of females and 34.2% of males), but far fewer sought help (12.5% of females and 3.2% of males) or received help (10.7% of females and 3.2% of males) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[10]</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, this cascade approach, well developed in HIV care, has not been applied to CSA at the population level across multiple LMICs.
Where survivors are lost along this cascade is unlikely to be random.

Current models treat disclosure as a social-ecological process, applying Bronfenbrenner's framework [29]: individual behavior is embedded in nested interpersonal, community, and societal systems, and disclosure is shaped by interacting individual, family, contextual, and cultural factors [22].
text.formatted: Current models treat disclosure as a social-ecological process, applying Bronfenbrenner's framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[29]</ref>: individual behavior is embedded in nested interpersonal, community, and societal systems, and disclosure is shaped by interacting individual, family, contextual, and cultural factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref>.

text.text: At the individual level, age, sex, age at first victimization, the relationship to the perpetrator, and the severity or repetition of abuse are associated with whether and to whom a child discloses.
At the family level, household structure and the quality of parental relationships shape access to a trusted confidant.
At the community level, social norms, stigma, and the availability of services influence whether disclosure leads to support or sanction [22, 23].
text.formatted: At the community level, social norms, stigma, and the availability of services influence whether disclosure leads to support or sanction <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">23]</ref>.

text.text: Sex differences are especially salient, with evidence that boys and girls face distinct disclosure dynamics [22].
text.formatted: Sex differences are especially salient, with evidence that boys and girls face distinct disclosure dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref>.

text.text: International frameworks such as INSPIRE, a package of seven strategies developed by the World Health Organization and nine partner agencies, identify response and support services as a core strategy for ending violence against children, alongside efforts to shift the social norms that inhibit disclosure [30].
text.formatted: International frameworks such as INSPIRE, a package of seven strategies developed by the World Health Organization and nine partner agencies, identify response and support services as a core strategy for ending violence against children, alongside efforts to shift the social norms that inhibit disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[30]</ref>.

text.text: However, reviews of disclosure research call for more evidence on environmental, contextual, and cultural factors [22] and for more robust study designs [23].
text.formatted: However, reviews of disclosure research call for more evidence on environmental, contextual, and cultural factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref> and for more robust study designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Even children's own understandings of violence may differ from the categories used in survey instruments [31].

text.text: The VACS offer a rare opportunity to address this gap: standardized, nationally representative, household-based surveys fielded across many LMICs, each capturing the disclosure-and-services cascade in a comparable way.

Pooling these surveys makes it possible to estimate the cascade across countries and to identify the factors associated with loss at each step with greater precision and generalizability than any single national study allows.
We pooled nationally representative VACS data from 15 LMICs to examine the CSA disclosure-and-services cascade among 18-to 24-year-olds who experienced sexual abuse before age 18.

We assessed three questions: (1) what proportion of survivors tell anyone, know where to seek formal help, seek help, and receive help, overall, by country, and by sex; (2) at which step the greatest loss occurs, and whether this pattern differs across countries and by sex; and (3) which individual-, family-, and community-level factors are associated with reaching each step.

text.text: By locating where survivors are lost along the cascade and identifying who is most likely to be lost, the analysis aims to inform where investment, whether in awareness, service access, or the norms that govern CSA disclosure, can most effectively reduce the gap between the occurrence of abuse and an effective response.

text.text: Surveys had to meet several pre-specified criteria to be included in this analysis.
The dataset had to be publicly available through Together for Girls and use the standardized VACS sexual violence and disclosure modules.
The sample had to be nationally representative and household-based, drawn through multistage cluster sampling, and include both sexes aged 13 to 24 interviewed by matched-sex staff.
Data collection had to occur in 2013 or later, when the VACS adopted standardized sexual violence and disclosure modules, making the surveys comparable.
The file had to contain the four CSA acts with their age-at-first-event items, the four cascade items or derivable equivalents, and the sampling weight, primary sampling unit (PSU), and stratum.

text.text: In all surveys, respondents aged 13 to 17 were included only in a sensitivity analysis (SA1) because their period of exposure before age 18 is incomplete.
CSA is defined as any of four acts before age 18, by any perpetrator: unwanted sexual touching, attempted forced sex, pressured or coerced sex, and physically forced sex.
In Honduras, El Salvador, and Moldova, the version of the pressured-sex question about partners also covers sex when the respondent was too drunk to say no.
Where a survey asks a separate question about sex while too drunk to refuse, that question was not counted.
An act was counted as occurring before age 18 when the reported age at the first occurrence was under 18.
When the age at the first occurrence was missing, the age at the most recent occurrence was used; acts with no usable age were not counted.
With this definition, our weighted prevalence estimates agree with all 30 sexspecific estimates in the published country reports to within 0.1 percentage point ( S1 Table).

text.text: The cascade has four steps, each coded 0 or 1 from the harmonized items: told anyone about the experience; knew of a place to go for help, such as a health facility, the police, or social services; sought help from such a service; and received help from a service.

In seven surveys, the questionnaire's list of places also includes community or religious leaders (Eswatini, Lesotho, Namibia, and Tanzania, and in the question on receiving help in Zimbabwe), nongovernmental organizations (NGOs; Lesotho, Nigeria, and Zambia), or teachers and faith-based organizations (Nigeria and Zambia); these were kept as recorded.
The survey routing shapes how the steps can be analyzed.
In most surveys, the question on seeking help is asked only of survivors who knew of a place to go, and the question on receiving help only of those who sought help.

We therefore analyzed the cascade as a sequence of conditional steps: telling and knowing among all survivors, seeking help among survivors who knew where to seek help, and receiving help among survivors who sought it.
Some survivors answered no to having told anyone but reported seeking or receiving help from a service.
Because a survivor cannot seek help from a service without telling someone, we counted seeking or receiving formal help as telling.
This changed the value for 39 survivors in the cascade denominator and raised the pooled proportion who told anyone from 45.5% to 47.1%.
In Malawi, Nigeria, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, survivors who received help were not asked the disclosure (telling anyone) question, so the self-report item was also set to 1 for them.
Because of this recoding, our estimates of disclosure (telling anyone) are not directly comparable with published country values.
Results based on the self-report item alone are presented as a sensitivity analysis.
Covariates were limited to those that could be harmonized across the surveys ( S2 Table) and were grouped by ecological level [22, 29].

text.text: Individual-level covariates were sex; age in years; highest level of schooling reached (none or less than primary, primary, secondary, or higher than secondary; for respondents still in school, the level they were attending); whether the respondent had ever married or lived with a partner; lifetime physical violence by a partner, peer, parent or caregiver, or adult in the community; and lifetime emotional violence by a parent or caregiver.
Family-level covariates included whether the biological mother and father were alive.
Communityand peer-level covariates were whether the respondent had seen someone attacked outside the home and family before age 18, and whether the respondent talks to friends about important things.

The peer item was coded 1 for a lot or some (a lot or a little in Malawi, Nigeria, and Zambia) and 0 for not very much or not at all; in Eswatini and Tanzania, it was coded 1 when the respondent agreed that they can talk about problems with friends.

Measures of community cohesion or trust, food insecurity, and closeness to parents were not asked in a comparable way in all surveys, and so were not included in the primary models; closeness to parents was examined in a sensitivity analysis.
According to the El Salvador codebook, the survey did not ask the peer item, so models that include it use 14 countries.

In Zimbabwe, the witnessing items were asked of a subsample only; respondents who were not asked (and 4 survivors who declined) were kept in the models with a separate indicator, which was not interpreted.

Each analysis incorporates the survey design through the sampling weight, PSU, and stratum, which are present in all 15 public-use files, except that the Lesotho and Zambia files have no design stratum; district (Lesotho) and province (Zambia) were used as the stratum.
PSUs were nested within strata within each country and were defined separately for females and males.
In the three surveys released as separate female and male files (Malawi, Nigeria, and Zambia), strata were also defined separately by sex.

text.text: We also report the overall proportions of all survivors who sought and who received help.

In these overall rates, seeking help is 0 when the respondent did not know of a service, and receiving help is 0 when help was not sought, whereas in the conditional steps these respondents are outside the denominator.
We checked every derived variable against the questionnaire and codebook for its survey.
All estimates account for the complex survey design (weights, strata, and PSUs), with variances estimated by Taylor-series linearization.
The raw VACS weights sum to each country's population, so pooled estimates on raw weights would be dominated by the most populous countries; Nigeria would contribute the largest share.
For pooled estimates, we therefore rescaled each respondent's weight so that the weights in each country sum to that country's sample size.
Each country then contributes in proportion to its sample, and country-specific estimates are unchanged.
Pooled estimates are thus a sample-weighted average of 15 surveys fielded between 2013 and 2024, not an estimate for the population of any region.

Estimates for subgroups, such as survivors or survivors who knew where to seek help, were computed as subpopulations of the full pooled design, so that all strata and PSUs contribute to the variance estimates.
We report 95% CIs on the logit scale, using the design degrees of freedom of each subpopulation.

text.text: To identify factors associated with each modeled step (telling, knowing, and seeking help among those who knew), we fitted logistic regression models that use the survey weights and design and include an indicator for each country (country fixed effects).
Because of these country indicators, we compare survivors within each country.
Differences between countries, such as the number of services available, the questionnaire version used, or when the survey took place, therefore do not affect the adjusted odds ratios (aORs).
We included sex as a covariate rather than stratifying the models, because only 27 male survivors sought help.
No interaction terms were fitted.
Age was entered as years above or below 21, the middle of the 18-24 range.
Centering does not change the odds ratio for age.
Models used complete cases for the outcome and all covariates (telling: n = 3,328; knowing: n = 3,350; seeking help among those who knew: n = 1,120; 14 countries).
Unadjusted and country-adjusted odds ratios in the same samples are given in S4 Table.

text.text: We describe receipt of help among those who sought it but do not model it, because it was high and based on few male cases.
As a supplementary analysis, we fitted multilevel logistic models that allow each country its own baseline level at each step.

From these models, we estimated the intraclass correlation (ICC): the share of the variation in each step, after adjustment for covariates and on the latent (logit) scale, that lies between countries rather than between individuals.
In these models, the survey weights were rescaled to sum to each country's sample size, and each country was given the same weight [37, 38].

With only 14 or 15 countries, their standard errors are likely to be too small and their estimates of between-country variation unstable [39, 40].

The lower odds of knowing where to seek help among female survivors were not present among survivors of forced or pressured sex (SA4: aOR 1.05, 0.63-1.74), and the associations of telling with having ever married or cohabited and with emotional violence by a parent or caregiver were not statistically significant at ages 13 to 24, in the six-survey subsample, or among survivors of forced or pressured sex.
Other associations were statistically significant in no more than three specifications ( S4 Table).
text.formatted: Other associations were statistically significant in no more than three specifications ( <ref type="table">S4</ref> Table).

text.text: Across 15 nationally representative surveys, fewer than half of young adults who had experienced sexual abuse in childhood had told anyone, about one in three knew where to seek formal help, and 7% had received formal help.
Most survivors were lost before they reached a service: at the step of knowing where to go, and at the step from knowing to seeking help.
Once survivors sought help, most received it.
The pattern differed by sex.
Female survivors were more likely to tell anyone and, once they knew where to seek help, to seek it.
Male survivors were at least as likely to know where to go but rarely sought help.
Age, schooling, and having a living mother were associated with knowing where to seek help, but no characteristic other than sex was associated with seeking it.
The low level of service receipt is consistent with earlier VACS analyses.

Across seven countries surveyed between 2007 and 2013, Sumner et al. [41] found that 10% or fewer of survivors of childhood sexual violence received services in most countries; we found the same order of magnitude in 12 of our 15 surveys, 14 of which were conducted after 2013.
text.formatted: Across seven countries surveyed between 2007 and 2013, Sumner et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[41]</ref> found that 10% or fewer of survivors of childhood sexual violence received services in most countries; we found the same order of magnitude in 12 of our 15 surveys, 14 of which were conducted after 2013.

text.text: The low rate is consistent with reviews of CSA disclosure, which find that many children do not disclose abuse or delay disclosure [23, 27].
text.formatted: The low rate is consistent with reviews of CSA disclosure, which find that many children do not disclose abuse or delay disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">27]</ref>.

text.text: The cascade adds information that prevalence and disclosure rates alone do not provide.
As in HIV care [28], the steps with the largest losses show where effort is most needed, although gains at one step are limited unless the later steps also improve.
text.formatted: As in HIV care <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[28]</ref>, the steps with the largest losses show where effort is most needed, although gains at one step are limited unless the later steps also improve.

text.text: Here, most losses occurred before survivors reached a service rather than within the service system.
The high receipt rate among survivors who sought help suggests that services usually respond when survivors reach them, although the surveys do not measure the quality of that response.
The cascade also varied widely between countries.

The proportion of survivors who received formal help ranged from 0.9% in Mozambique to 26.3% in Eswatini, and after adjustment for individual characteristics, between-country differences accounted for 6% to 18% of the latent variation at each modeled step, with the largest share at the step of seeking help.
The overall pattern nevertheless held in every country: in no country did more than 60% of survivors know where to seek help, or more than half of those who knew seek it.
The surveys cannot explain these differences, which may reflect service availability, questionnaire version, or survey year, so comparisons between individual countries should be made with caution.
The sex differences are consistent with evidence that boys and girls face different barriers to disclosure [22].
text.formatted: The sex differences are consistent with evidence that boys and girls face different barriers to disclosure <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[22]</ref>.

text.text: In our data, male survivors were at least as likely as female survivors to know where to seek help, yet far fewer sought it.
For males, the main barrier therefore appears to be the step from knowing to acting rather than a lack of information.

This pattern is consistent with a systematic review of help-seeking for mental health problems among adolescent boys and young men, mostly in high-income countries, which identified conformity to masculine norms such as self-reliance and emotional stoicism, self-stigma, limited information about where to get help, and practical barriers such as the location, time, and cost of services [42].
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with a systematic review of help-seeking for mental health problems among adolescent boys and young men, mostly in high-income countries, which identified conformity to masculine norms such as self-reliance and emotional stoicism, self-stigma, limited information about where to get help, and practical barriers such as the location, time, and cost of services <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[42]</ref>.

text.text: The lower odds of knowing among female survivors were not present among survivors of forced or pressured sex, which suggests that this difference partly reflects differences in the type of abuse that female and male survivors reported.

The association between schooling and knowing where to seek help is consistent with schools being a source of information about services, and the association with having a living mother suggests that a parent may be a route to that information.
Survivors who had ever married or lived with a partner were less likely to have told anyone.

Telling may carry a higher social cost for survivors who are married or living with a partner, which could discourage disclosure, but the cross-sectional data cannot show whether the abuse, the disclosure, or the marriage came first.
Three implications follow.
First, services must be known: two in three survivors did not know where to seek help.

INSPIRE's response-and-support strategy calls for well-publicized, accessible mechanisms through which children can seek help [30]; such services work only if children and young people know they exist.
text.formatted: INSPIRE's response-and-support strategy calls for well-publicized, accessible mechanisms through which children can seek help <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[30]</ref>; such services work only if children and young people know they exist.

text.text: Information delivered through schools and communities could reach many of them, and the schooling gradient suggests that young people with little schooling need other channels.
Second, knowledge alone is not enough, especially for young men: three in four survivors who knew where to go did not seek help, and among male survivors nearly nine in ten did not.
Services and messages may need to address confidentiality, stigma, gender norms, and the specific barriers that male survivors face.

Third, because disclosure is often delayed, sometimes for many years [25] [26] [27], services and legal remedies should remain available to survivors who seek help long after the abuse, including through reforms to extend or eliminate civil and criminal statutes of limitations where necessary.
text.formatted: Third, because disclosure is often delayed, sometimes for many years <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[25]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[26]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[27]</ref>, services and legal remedies should remain available to survivors who seek help long after the abuse, including through reforms to extend or eliminate civil and criminal statutes of limitations where necessary.

text.text: To our knowledge, this is the first analysis of the full CSA disclosure-and-services cascade that pools nationally representative surveys from many LMICs.
The surveys share a common core instrument, and we documented item-by-item harmonization for each survey.
Our prevalence estimates reproduce the published country estimates.
All estimates use the full survey design.

The sex difference in disclosure (telling anyone) was in the same direction in all nine sensitivity specifications, and the sex difference in seeking help in all eight that modeled it, although some other associations depended on the specification.
Several limitations apply.
First, the data are cross-sectional and self-reported; recall and the willingness to report abuse and help-seeking may differ by sex and by country.
Second, the surveys differ in year (2013 to 2024) and in instrument version, and the harmonized items are not identical across surveys.
Country fixed effects remove stable differences between countries but not differences in how individual items perform.

In some surveys, the list of formal services includes community or religious leaders, NGOs, or teachers; El Salvador's "basic" schooling category (grades 1 to 9 in the questionnaire) spans primary and lower secondary levels, and in three surveys the version of the pressured-sex question about partners also covers sex while too drunk to say no.

Third, in Lesotho the cascade covers only survivors of forced or pressured sex, and in Moldova the question on telling was not asked of some survivors because of a routing error noted in the country report [13].
text.formatted: Third, in Lesotho the cascade covers only survivors of forced or pressured sex, and in Moldova the question on telling was not asked of some survivors because of a routing error noted in the country report <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, the cascade questions refer to any of a survivor's experiences, not a specific incident, and the surveys do not record the order of events, such as whether telling preceded learning about services.
Fifth, only 27 male survivors sought help, so estimates for this step among males are imprecise, and most male estimates could not be reported for six countries.
Sixth, the pooled estimates weight countries by sample size and do not represent the population of any region.

Seventh, the models used complete cases, which excluded 7% to 8% of survivors at each modeled step, including all 89 survivors in El Salvador, where the peer item was not asked; models without the peer item, fitted to all 15 surveys, gave similar results ( S4 Table).
text.formatted: Seventh, the models used complete cases, which excluded 7% to 8% of survivors at each modeled step, including all 89 survivors in El Salvador, where the peer item was not asked; models without the peer item, fitted to all 15 surveys, gave similar results ( <ref type="table">S4</ref> Table).

text.text: Finally, the surveys do not measure when survivors first disclosed, the quality of the services received, or whether the help met survivors' needs.
Data on the timing of disclosure are needed to measure delay directly.
Studies of service quality, and of why survivors who know about services do not use them, especially young men, would help design better responses.
Qualitative research could clarify how marriage and family structure shape disclosure.
Because the VACS are repeated, future surveys could also show whether the cascade changes over time, as repeated surveys have shown for the prevalence of violence against children in Kenya [43].
text.formatted: Because the VACS are repeated, future surveys could also show whether the cascade changes over time, as repeated surveys have shown for the prevalence of violence against children in Kenya <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[43]</ref>.

text.text: Across 15 countries, most young people who experienced sexual abuse in childhood never reached a formal service.
The largest losses occurred before survivors reached services: most did not know where to go, and most who knew did not seek help.
Telling someone is not enough: 47% of survivors told someone, but only 7% received formal help.

Policies should make services known to young people, particularly those with less schooling, and reduce the barriers that keep survivors, especially young men, from using the services they know about.
